In the light of the Way, these are called leftover food and useless growths. Things may detest them, so one who has the Way does not dwell in them.

t: There was a thing formed in chaos, born before heaven and…
y: 有物混成，先天地生。寂兮寥兮，獨立不改，周行而不殆，可以為天下母。吾不知其名，字之曰道，强為之名曰大。大曰逝，逝曰遠，遠曰反。故道大，天大，地大，王亦大。域中有四大，而王居其一焉。人法地，地法天，天法道，道法自然。
x: There was a thing formed in chaos, born before heaven and earth. Silent and empty, standing alone and unchanging, going round everywhere without danger, it can be the mother of the world. I do not know its name; I style it "the Way," and forced to name it, I call it "great." Great means going on; going on means far away; far away means turning back. So the Way is great, heaven is great, earth is great, and the king too is great. Within the realm there are four great ones, and the king is one of them. Man follows earth, earth follows heaven, heaven follows the Way, and the Way follows what is so of itself.

t: The heavy is the root of the light
y: 重為輕根，靜為躁君。是以聖人終日行不離輜重。雖有榮觀，燕處超然。奈何萬乘之主，而以身輕天下？輕則失本，躁則失君。
x: The heavy is the root of the light; stillness is the lord of restlessness. Therefore the sage travels all day without leaving his baggage cart. Though there are splendid sights, he stays at ease above them. How can the lord of ten thousand chariots treat his own person lightly before the world? Light, and he loses the root; restless, and he loses his lordship.

t: A good traveler leaves no tracks
y: 善行無轍迹，善言無瑕謫，善數不用籌策，善閉無關楗而不可開，善結無繩約而不可解。是以聖人常善救人，故無棄人；常善救物，故無棄物，是謂襲明。故善人者，不善人之師；不善人者，善人之資。不貴其師，不愛其資，雖智大迷，是謂要妙。
x: A good traveler leaves no tracks; a good speaker makes no slips; a good counter needs no tallies; a good closer needs no bolt, yet what he shuts cannot be opened; a good binder needs no rope, yet what he ties cannot be undone. Therefore the sage is always good at saving people, so no one is cast away; always good at saving things, so nothing is cast away. This is called following the light. So the good man is the teacher of the not-good, and the not-good is the material of the good. Not to value one's teacher, not to love one's material, though clever, is to be greatly lost. This is called the essential mystery.

t: Know the male, keep to the female, and be the ravine of the…
y: 知其雄，守其雌，為天下谿。為天下谿，常德不離，復歸於嬰兒。知其白，守其黑，為天下式。為天下式，常德不忒，復歸於無極。知其榮，守其辱，為天下谷。為天下谷，常德乃足，復歸於樸。樸散則為器，聖人用之則為官長，故大制不割。
x: Know the male, keep to the female, and be the ravine of the world. Being the ravine of the world, constant virtue never leaves, and one returns to being an infant. Know the white, keep to the black, and be the model of the world. Being the model of the world, constant virtue never errs, and one returns to the limitless. Know glory, keep to disgrace, and be the valley of the world. Being the valley of the world, constant virtue is sufficient, and one returns to the uncarved block. When the uncarved block is split, it becomes vessels; the sage uses them and becomes head of the officials. So the great cutting does not cut.

t: One who wants to take the world and work on it, I see that…
y: 將欲取天下而為之，吾見其不得已。天下神器，不可為也。為者敗之，執者失之。故物或行或隨，或歔或吹，或强或羸，或挫或隳。是以聖人去甚，去奢，去泰。
x: One who wants to take the world and work on it, I see that he will not succeed. The world is a sacred vessel; it cannot be worked on. Whoever works on it ruins it; whoever grasps it loses it. So among things some lead and some follow, some breathe gently and some blow hard, some are strong and some weak, some break and some fall. Therefore the sage avoids the extreme, the extravagant, and the excessive.

t: One who assists a ruler with the Way does not use arms to…
y: 以道佐人主者，不以兵强天下，其事好還。師之所處，荊棘生焉；大軍之後，必有凶年。善有果而已，不敢以取强。果而勿矜，果而勿伐，果而勿驕，果而不得已，果而勿强。物壯則老，是謂不道，不道早已。
x: One who assists a ruler with the Way does not use arms to force his will on the world; such deeds tend to rebound. Where armies have camped, thorns and brambles grow; after great wars, bad years are sure to follow. The good general achieves his aim and stops; he does not dare to use it to seize power. He achieves his aim but does not brag, achieves it but does not boast, achieves it but is not arrogant, achieves it because he had no choice, achieves it but does not force. Things in their prime grow old; this is called not following the Way, and what does not follow the Way soon ends.

t: Fine weapons are instruments of ill omen
y: 夫佳兵者，不祥之器，物或惡之，故有道者不處。君子居則貴左，用兵則貴右。兵者不祥之器，非君子之器，不得已而用之，恬淡為上。勝而不美，而美之者，是樂殺人。夫樂殺人者，則不可以得志於天下矣。吉事尚左，凶事尚右。偏將軍居左，上將軍居右，言以喪禮處之。殺人之衆，以哀悲泣之；戰勝，以喪禮處之。
x: Fine weapons are instruments of ill omen; things may detest them, so one who has the Way does not dwell with them. The gentleman at home honors the left; in war he honors the right. Weapons are instruments of ill omen, not the instruments of a gentleman; he uses them only when he has no choice, and calm restraint is best. Victory is not a thing to admire; to admire it is to delight in killing. One who delights in killing cannot have his way in the world. In happy affairs the left is honored; in sad affairs the right. The lieutenant general stands on the left, the commanding general on the right: that is, they are placed as at a funeral. When many people have been killed, mourn them with grief and tears; a victory in war is observed with funeral rites.

t: The Way is constant and nameless
y: 道常無名。樸雖小，天下莫能臣也。侯王若能守之，萬物將自賓。天地相合，以降甘露，民莫之令而自均。始制有名，名亦既有，夫亦將知止，知止可以不殆。譬道之在天下，猶川谷之於江海。
x: The Way is constant and nameless. The uncarved block, though small, no one in the world can make a subject of it. If lords and kings could keep to it, the ten thousand things would come as guests of their own accord. Heaven and earth unite and send down sweet dew; with no one ordering them, the people share it evenly by themselves. Once the uncarved is cut, there are names; once there are names, one should know when to stop; knowing when to stop, one can avoid danger. The Way in the world is like rivers and streams flowing to the rivers and the sea.

t: One who knows others is clever
y: 知人者智，自知者明。勝人者有力，自勝者强。知足者富，强行者有志。不失其所者久，死而不亡者壽。
x: One who knows others is clever; one who knows himself is clear-sighted. One who conquers others has strength; one who conquers himself is strong. One who knows contentment is rich; one who acts with persistence has will. One who does not lose his place endures; one who dies but is not forgotten lives long.

t: The great Way flows everywhere
y: 大道氾兮，其可左右。萬物恃之而生而不辭，功成不名有，衣養萬物而不為主。常無欲，可名於小；萬物歸焉而不為主，可名為大。以其終不自為大，故能成其大。
x: The great Way flows everywhere; it can go left or right. The ten thousand things depend on it for life, and it does not turn them away; its work done, it claims no name; it clothes and nourishes the ten thousand things but does not act as their master. Ever without desire, it can be called small; the ten thousand things return to it, yet it does not act as their master, and it can be called great. Because to the end it never makes itself great, it can achieve greatness.

t: Hold to the great image and the world will come
y: 執大象，天下往。往而不害，安平太。樂與餌，過客止。道之出口，淡乎其無味，視之不足見，聽之不足聞，用之不足既。
x: Hold to the great image and the world will come. It comes and meets no harm, but peace, calm, and ease. Music and food make passing travelers stop. But the Way, when spoken, is bland and has no flavor; looked at, it is not enough to see; listened to, it is not enough to hear; used, it cannot be used up.

t: What is to be shrunk must first be stretched
y: 將欲歙之，必固張之；將欲弱之，必固强之；將欲廢之，必固興之；將欲奪之，必固與之。是謂微明。柔弱勝剛强。魚不可脫於淵，國之利器不可以示人。
x: What is to be shrunk must first be stretched; what is to be weakened must first be strengthened; what is to be abolished must first be raised up; what is to be taken must first be given. This is called subtle insight. The soft and weak overcome the hard and strong. Fish must not leave the deep; the sharp instruments of the state must not be shown to people.

t: The Way is constantly without contrivance, yet nothing is…
y: 道常無為而無不為。侯王若能守之，萬物將自化。化而欲作，吾將鎮之以無名之樸。無名之樸，夫亦將無欲。不欲以靜，天下將自定。
x: The Way is constantly without contrivance, yet nothing is left undone. If lords and kings could keep to it, the ten thousand things would transform of themselves. If, transformed, they wish to stir, I will settle them with the nameless uncarved block. The nameless uncarved block brings freedom from desire. Without desire and so at rest, the world will settle of itself.

t: Superior virtue is not virtuous, and so it has virtue
y: 上德不德，是以有德；下德不失德，是以無德。上德無為而無以為，下德為之而有以為。上仁為之而無以為，上義為之而有以為，上禮為之而莫之應，則攘臂而扔之。故失道而後德，失德而後仁，失仁而後義，失義而後禮。夫禮者，忠信之薄而亂之首。前識者，道之華而愚之始。是以大丈夫處其厚，不居其薄；處其實，不居其華。故去彼取此。
x: Superior virtue is not virtuous, and so it has virtue; inferior virtue never lets go of virtue, and so it has no virtue. Superior virtue does nothing and has no motive for doing; inferior virtue acts and has a motive for acting. Superior humaneness acts but has no motive; superior righteousness acts and has a motive; superior ritual acts, and when no one responds, it rolls up its sleeves and drags them along. So when the Way is lost there is virtue; when virtue is lost, humaneness; when humaneness is lost, righteousness; when righteousness is lost, ritual. Ritual is the thinning of loyalty and trust and the beginning of disorder. Foreknowledge is the flower of the Way and the beginning of folly. Therefore the great man dwells in the thick, not the thin; in the fruit, not the flower. So he rejects that and takes this.

t: Of old, these attained the One
y: 昔之得一者：天得一以清，地得一以寧，神得一以靈，谷得一以盈，萬物得一以生，侯王得一以為天下貞。其致之。天無以清將恐裂，地無以寧將恐發，神無以靈將恐歇，谷無以盈將恐竭，萬物無以生將恐滅，侯王無以貴高將恐蹶。故貴以賤為本，高以下為基。是以侯王自謂孤、寡、不轂。此非以賤為本耶？非乎？故致數輿無輿。不欲琭琭如玉，珞珞如石。
x: Of old, these attained the One: heaven attained the One and became clear; earth attained the One and became steady; the spirits attained the One and became potent; the valley attained the One and became full; the ten thousand things attained the One and came to life; lords and kings attained the One and became the standard of the world. It is the One that brought this about. Were heaven not clear, it might split; were earth not steady, it might quake; were the spirits not potent, they might fade; were the valley not full, it might run dry; were the ten thousand things not alive, they might perish; were lords and kings not honored and high, they might fall. So the noble has the humble as its root, and the high has the low as its base. That is why lords and kings call themselves the orphan, the widower, the unworthy. Is this not taking the humble as root? Is it not? So count the parts of a carriage and there is no carriage. Do not wish to glitter like jade; be plain like stone.

t: Turning back is the movement of the Way
y: 反者道之動，弱者道之用。天下萬物生於有，有生於無。
x: Turning back is the movement of the Way; weakness is the use of the Way. The things of the world are born from being, and being is born from non-being.

t: When the best scholars hear of the Way, they practice it…
y: 上士聞道，勤而行之；中士聞道，若存若亡；下士聞道，大笑之。不笑不足以為道。故建言有之：明道若昧，進道若退，夷道若纇，上德若谷，大白若辱，廣德若不足，建德若偷，質真若渝，大方無隅，大器晚成，大音希聲，大象無形。道隱無名。夫唯道，善貸且成。
x: When the best scholars hear of the Way, they practice it diligently. When middling scholars hear of the Way, they half keep it and half lose it. When the lowest scholars hear of the Way, they laugh out loud. If they did not laugh, it would not be the Way. So the established sayings have it: the bright Way seems dim; the Way forward seems to go back; the level Way seems rough; the highest virtue seems like a valley; the purest white seems soiled; ample virtue seems insufficient; firm virtue seems furtive; true substance seems to change; the great square has no corners; the great vessel is finished late; the great sound is faint; the great image has no shape. The Way is hidden and nameless. Only the Way is good at lending and at bringing to completion.

t: The Way gives birth to one, one gives birth to two, two…
y: 道生一，一生二，二生三，三生萬物。萬物負陰而抱陽，沖氣以為和。人之所惡，唯孤、寡、不穀，而王公以為稱。故物或損之而益，或益之而損。人之所教，我亦教之。强梁者不得其死，吾將以為教父。
x: The Way gives birth to one, one gives birth to two, two gives birth to three, and three gives birth to the ten thousand things. The ten thousand things carry yin on their backs and embrace yang, and the blending of their breaths makes harmony. What people dislike is to be orphaned, widowed, or unworthy, yet kings and lords use these to name themselves. So things are sometimes increased by being diminished, and sometimes diminished by being increased. What others teach, I teach too: the violent do not die a natural death. I will take this as the father of my teaching.

t: The softest thing in the world gallops through the hardest
y: 天下之至柔，馳騁天下之至堅。無有入無間，吾是以知無為之有益。不言之教，無為之益，天下希及之。
x: The softest thing in the world gallops through the hardest. What has no substance enters where there is no gap. From this I know the benefit of doing without contrivance. The teaching without words and the benefit of doing without contrivance: few in the world attain them.

t: Your name or your life
y: 名與身孰親？身與貨孰多？得與亡孰病？是故甚愛必大費，多藏必厚亡。知足不辱，知止不殆，可以長久。
x: Your name or your life: which is dearer? Your life or your goods: which is worth more? Gain or loss: which is the harm? So excessive love must lead to great expense, and much hoarding must lead to heavy loss. Know contentment and you will not be disgraced; know when to stop and you will be in no danger; you can then last long.

t: Great perfection seems lacking, yet its use never wears out
y: 大成若缺，其用不弊。大盈若沖，其用不窮。大直若屈，大巧若拙，大辯若訥。躁勝寒，靜勝熱，清靜為天下正。
x: Great perfection seems lacking, yet its use never wears out. Great fullness seems empty, yet its use is never exhausted. Great straightness seems bent; great skill seems clumsy; great eloquence seems tongue-tied. Restless movement overcomes cold; stillness overcomes heat. Clear stillness is the standard of the world.

t: When the world has the Way, galloping horses are turned…
y: 天下有道，卻走馬以糞；天下無道，戎馬生於郊。禍莫大於不知足，咎莫大於欲得。故知足之足，常足矣。
x: When the world has the Way, galloping horses are turned back to haul manure. When the world lacks the Way, warhorses are bred on the borders. No disaster is greater than not knowing contentment; no fault is greater than the wish to acquire. So the contentment of knowing contentment is lasting contentment.

t: Without going out the door, one knows the world
y: 不出戶，知天下；不闚牖，見天道。其出彌遠，其知彌少。是以聖人不行而知，不見而名，不為而成。
x: Without going out the door, one knows the world; without looking out the window, one sees the Way of heaven. The farther one goes, the less one knows. Therefore the sage knows without traveling, names things without seeing them, and accomplishes without acting.

t: In pursuing learning, one adds every day
y: 為學日益，為道日損。損之又損，以至於無為，無為而無不為。取天下常以無事，及其有事，不足以取天下。
x: In pursuing learning, one adds every day; in pursuing the Way, one sheds every day. Shed and shed again, until one reaches doing without contrivance; doing without contrivance, nothing is left undone. To win the world, always be free of meddling; once you meddle, you are not fit to win the world.

t: The sage has no fixed mind of his own
y: 聖人無常心，以百姓心為心。善者吾善之，不善者吾亦善之，德善。信者吾信之，不信者吾亦信之，德信。聖人在天下歙歙，為天下渾其心，聖人皆孩之。
x: The sage has no fixed mind of his own; he takes the people's minds as his mind. Those who are good, I treat as good; those who are not good, I also treat as good; and so goodness is attained. Those who are trustworthy, I trust; those who are not trustworthy, I also trust; and so trust is attained. The sage in the world is cautious and withdrawn, and for the world's sake he muddles his mind. The people all fix their eyes and ears on him, and the sage treats them all as children.

t: Coming out into life, going in to death
y: 出生入死。生之徒十有三，死之徒十有三，人之生動之死地亦十有三。夫何故？以其生生之厚。蓋聞善攝生者，陸行不遇兕虎，入軍不被甲兵。兕無所投其角，虎無所措其爪，兵無所容其刃。夫何故？以其無死地。
x: Coming out into life, going in to death. Followers of life are three in ten; followers of death are three in ten; and those who live but by their own moves go to the place of death are also three in ten. Why is this? Because they cling too hard to life. I have heard that one good at preserving life travels on land without meeting rhinoceros or tiger, and goes into battle without wearing armor or carrying weapons. The rhinoceros finds nowhere to drive its horn, the tiger nowhere to set its claws, the weapon nowhere to lodge its blade. Why is this? Because he has no place of death.

t: The Way gives them life, virtue rears them, things give…
y: 道生之，德畜之，物形之，勢成之。是以萬物莫不尊道而貴德。道之尊，德之貴，夫莫之命而常自然。故道生之，德畜之，長之育之，亭之毒之，養之覆之。生而不有，為而不恃，長而不宰，是謂玄德。
x: The Way gives them life, virtue rears them, things give them shape, circumstances complete them. So the ten thousand things all honor the Way and prize virtue. The Way is honored and virtue prized not because anyone commands it, but always of their own accord. So the Way gives them life and virtue rears them; it raises them and nurtures them, settles them and matures them, feeds them and shelters them. It gives life but does not possess, acts but does not rely on it, raises but does not rule. This is called dark virtue.

t: The world has a beginning, which may be taken as the mother…
y: 天下有始，以為天下母。既得其母，以知其子；既知其子，復守其母，沒身不殆。塞其兌，閉其門，終身不勤。開其兌，濟其事，終身不救。見小曰明，守柔曰强。用其光，復歸其明，無遺身殃，是為習常。
x: The world has a beginning, which may be taken as the mother of the world. Having found the mother, one knows the children; knowing the children, one holds again to the mother, and to the end of life one is in no danger. Block the openings, shut the doors, and to the end of your life you will not be worn out. Open the openings, pursue your affairs, and to the end of your life you will not be saved. Seeing the small is called clarity; keeping to the soft is called strength. Use the light, return to clarity, and bring no harm upon yourself. This is called practicing the constant.

t: If I had even a little knowledge, walking on the great Way…
y: 使我介然有知，行於大道，唯施是畏。大道甚夷，而民好徑。朝甚除，田甚蕪，倉甚虛；服文綵，帶利劍，厭飲食，財貨有餘，是謂盜夸。非道也哉！
x: If I had even a little knowledge, walking on the great Way, I would fear only going astray. The great Way is very level, yet people love byways. The court is spotless, the fields are full of weeds, the granaries are empty; yet they wear embroidered clothes, carry sharp swords, are sated with food and drink, and have wealth to spare. This is called the boast of robbers. It is not the Way!

t: What is well planted cannot be uprooted
y: 善建者不拔，善抱者不脫，子孫以祭祀不輟。修之於身，其德乃真；修之於家，其德乃餘；修之於鄉，其德乃長；修之於國，其德乃豐；修之於天下，其德乃普。故以身觀身，以家觀家，以鄉觀鄉，以國觀國，以天下觀天下。吾何以知天下然哉？以此。
x: What is well planted cannot be uprooted; what is well held cannot slip away; and descendants will keep up the ancestral offerings without end. Cultivate it in yourself and your virtue will be genuine; cultivate it in your family and your virtue will be abundant; cultivate it in your village and your virtue will endure; cultivate it in your state and your virtue will flourish; cultivate it in the world and your virtue will be universal. So observe the self by the self, the family by the family, the village by the village, the state by the state, the world by the world. How do I know the world is so? By this.

t: One who holds virtue in its fullness is like a newborn child
y: 含德之厚，比於赤子。蜂蠆虺蛇不螫，猛獸不據，攫鳥不搏。骨弱筋柔而握固，未知牝牡之合而全作，精之至也。終日號而不嗄，和之至也。知和曰常，知常曰明，益生曰祥，心使氣曰强。物壯則老，謂之不道，不道早已。
x: One who holds virtue in its fullness is like a newborn child. Wasps, scorpions, and snakes do not sting him; wild beasts do not seize him; birds of prey do not strike him. His bones are weak and his sinews soft, yet his grip is firm. He does not yet know the union of male and female, yet he is fully aroused: this is the height of vitality. He cries all day without growing hoarse: this is the height of harmony. Knowing harmony is called the constant; knowing the constant is called clarity. Forcing life is called ill-omened; the mind driving the breath is called forcing. Things in their prime grow old; this is called not following the Way, and what does not follow the Way soon ends.

t: One who knows does not speak
y: 知者不言，言者不知。塞其兌，閉其門，挫其銳，解其分，和其光，同其塵，是謂玄同。故不可得而親，不可得而疏；不可得而利，不可得而害；不可得而貴，不可得而賤。故為天下貴。
x: One who knows does not speak; one who speaks does not know. Block the openings, shut the doors, blunt the sharp, untie the tangled, soften the glare, mingle with the dust: this is called dark sameness. So one cannot get close to him, nor keep him at a distance; one cannot benefit him, nor harm him; one cannot ennoble him, nor debase him. So he is the most honored in the world.

t: Govern the state with rectitude, use troops with surprise…
y: 以正治國，以奇用兵，以無事取天下。吾何以知其然哉？以此。天下多忌諱，而民彌貧；民多利器，國家滋昏；人多伎巧，奇物滋起；法令滋彰，盜賊多有。故聖人云：我無為而民自化，我好靜而民自正，我無事而民自富，我無欲而民自樸。
x: Govern the state with rectitude, use troops with surprise, win the world by not meddling. How do I know it is so? By this. The more prohibitions in the world, the poorer the people; the more sharp tools among the people, the more the state is in confusion; the more skill and cunning people have, the more strange things appear; the more laws and orders are displayed, the more thieves and robbers there are. So the sage says: I do nothing, and the people transform themselves; I love stillness, and the people correct themselves; I do not meddle, and the people prosper themselves; I have no desires, and the people become simple themselves.

t: When government is dull and muddled, the people are honest…
y: 其政悶悶，其民淳淳；其政察察，其民缺缺。禍兮福之所倚，福兮禍之所伏。孰知其極？其無正。正復為奇，善復為妖。人之迷，其日固久。是以聖人方而不割，廉而不劌，直而不肆，光而不燿。
x: When government is dull and muddled, the people are honest and simple; when government is sharp and prying, the people are wanting. Misfortune is what good fortune leans on; good fortune is where misfortune hides. Who knows where it ends? There is no fixed rule. The correct turns again into the strange, the good turns again into the uncanny. People have been confused about this for a very long time. Therefore the sage is square but does not cut, sharp-edged but does not wound, straight but does not overreach, bright but does not dazzle.

t: In governing people and serving heaven, nothing is better…
y: 治人事天莫若嗇。夫唯嗇，是謂早服。早服謂之重積德。重積德則無不克，無不克則莫知其極。莫知其極，可以有國。有國之母，可以長久。是謂深根固柢、長生久視之道。
x: In governing people and serving heaven, nothing is better than frugality. Only frugality means submitting early. Submitting early means accumulating virtue again and again. Accumulating virtue again and again, there is nothing one cannot overcome; when there is nothing one cannot overcome, no one knows one's limits; when no one knows one's limits, one can hold a state. Holding the mother of the state, one can last long. This is called the Way of deep roots and firm stems, of long life and lasting vision.

t: Governing a great state is like cooking a small fish
y: 治大國若烹小鮮。以道蒞天下，其鬼不神。非其鬼不神，其神不傷人；非其神不傷人，聖人亦不傷人。夫兩不相傷，故德交歸焉。
x: Governing a great state is like cooking a small fish. When the Way is used to oversee the world, ghosts lose their spirit power. It is not that the ghosts lose their power, but that their power does not harm people; it is not only that their power does not harm people, the sage also does not harm people. Since neither harms the other, their virtue flows back to the people together.

t: A great state is the lower reaches of a river, where the…
y: 大國者下流，天下之交，天下之牝。牝常以靜勝牡，以靜為下。故大國以下小國，則取小國；小國以下大國，則取大國。故或下以取，或下而取。大國不過欲兼畜人，小國不過欲入事人。夫兩者各得其所欲，大者宜為下。
x: A great state is the lower reaches of a river, where the world meets, the female of the world. The female always overcomes the male by stillness, and by stillness takes the lower place. So a great state, by placing itself below a small state, wins the small state; a small state, by placing itself below a great state, wins over the great state. So one wins by taking the lower place, the other wins by being in the lower place. The great state wishes no more than to unite and shelter others; the small state wishes no more than to join and serve others. For both to get what they want, the great one should take the lower place.

t: The Way is the hidden refuge of the ten thousand things…
y: 道者萬物之奧，善人之寶，不善人之所保。美言可以市，尊行可以加人。人之不善，何棄之有？故立天子，置三公，雖有拱璧以先駟馬，不如坐進此道。古之所以貴此道者何？不曰以求得，有罪以免耶？故為天下貴。
x: The Way is the hidden refuge of the ten thousand things, the treasure of the good, and what keeps the not-good safe. Fine words can be sold in the market; honorable conduct can raise a person above others. Even if people are not good, why cast them away? So when the Son of Heaven is enthroned and the three ministers installed, though one presents a jade disc followed by a team of four horses, it is not as good as sitting still and offering this Way. Why did the ancients prize this Way? Did they not say that by it one who seeks shall find, and one who has offended shall be spared? So it is the most honored in the world.

t: Act without contrivance, work without meddling, taste the…
y: 為無為，事無事，味無味。大小多少，報怨以德。圖難於其易，為大於其細。天下難事必作於易，天下大事必作於細。是以聖人終不為大，故能成其大。夫輕諾必寡信，多易必多難。是以聖人猶難之，故終無難矣。
x: Act without contrivance, work without meddling, taste the flavorless. Treat the small as great and the few as many; repay resentment with virtue. Plan the difficult while it is easy; do the great while it is small. The difficult things of the world must begin with the easy; the great things of the world must begin with the small. Therefore the sage never attempts the great, and so can achieve greatness. Light promises surely inspire little trust; taking much as easy surely brings much difficulty. Therefore even the sage treats things as difficult, and so in the end has no difficulty.

t: What is at rest is easy to hold
y: 其安易持，其未兆易謀，其脆易泮，其微易散。為之於未有，治之於未亂。合抱之木，生於毫末；九層之臺，起於累土；千里之行，始於足下。為者敗之，執者失之。是以聖人無為故無敗，無執故無失。民之從事，常於幾成而敗之。慎終如始，則無敗事。是以聖人欲不欲，不貴難得之貨；學不學，復衆人之所過，以輔萬物之自然而不敢為。
x: What is at rest is easy to hold; what has not yet shown signs is easy to plan for; what is brittle is easy to break; what is minute is easy to scatter. Deal with it before it exists; put it in order before disorder arises. A tree as wide as a man's embrace grows from a tiny shoot; a terrace of nine stories rises from a heap of earth; a journey of a thousand miles begins beneath one's feet. Whoever works on it ruins it; whoever grasps it loses it. Therefore the sage does not contrive and so does not fail; does not grasp and so does not lose. People in their undertakings often fail when they are on the verge of success. Be as careful at the end as at the beginning, and there will be no failure. Therefore the sage desires not to desire and does not prize goods hard to get; learns not to learn and brings people back from where they went too far. He helps the ten thousand things to be as they are of themselves and does not dare to contrive.

t: Those of old who were good at practicing the Way did not…
y: 古之善為道者，非以明民，將以愚之。民之難治，以其智多。故以智治國，國之賊；不以智治國，國之福。知此兩者亦稽式。常知稽式，是謂玄德。玄德深矣，遠矣，與物反矣，然後乃至大順。
x: Those of old who were good at practicing the Way did not use it to make the people clever, but to keep them simple. The people are hard to govern because they have too much cunning. So governing a state by cunning is a curse to the state; not governing a state by cunning is a blessing to the state. Knowing these two is also knowing the pattern. Always knowing the pattern is called dark virtue. Dark virtue is deep, it is far-reaching; it turns back with things, and then attains great accord.

t: The rivers and the sea can be kings of the hundred valleys…
y: 江海所以能為百谷王者，以其善下之，故能為百谷王。是以欲上民，必以言下之；欲先民，必以身後之。是以聖人處上而民不重，處前而民不害。是以天下樂推而不厭。以其不爭，故天下莫能與之爭。
x: The rivers and the sea can be kings of the hundred valleys because they are good at staying below them; so they can be kings of the hundred valleys. Therefore one who wishes to be above the people must speak as if below them; one who wishes to lead the people must put himself behind them. So the sage is above, and the people do not feel his weight; he is in front, and the people do not feel harmed. So the world gladly pushes him forward and never tires of him. Because he does not contend, no one in the world can contend with him.

t: All the world says my Way is great but seems unlike anything
y: 天下皆謂我道大，似不肖。夫唯大，故似不肖。若肖，久矣其細也夫！我有三寶，持而保之：一曰慈，二曰儉，三曰不敢為天下先。慈故能勇，儉故能廣，不敢為天下先故能成器長。今舍慈且勇，舍儉且廣，舍後且先，死矣！夫慈，以戰則勝，以守則固。天將救之，以慈衛之。
x: All the world says my Way is great but seems unlike anything. It is precisely because it is great that it seems unlike anything. Were it like something, it would long since have become petty. I have three treasures which I hold and keep: the first is compassion, the second is frugality, the third is not daring to be first in the world. Compassionate, one can be brave; frugal, one can be generous; not daring to be first in the world, one can become head of the officials. Now to be brave while forsaking compassion, generous while forsaking frugality, first while forsaking the last place: that is death! Compassion wins in battle and holds firm in defense. When heaven means to save someone, it guards him with compassion.

t: One good at being an officer is not warlike
y: 善為士者不武，善戰者不怒，善勝敵者不與，善用人者為之下。是謂不爭之德，是謂用人之力，是謂配天古之極。
x: One good at being an officer is not warlike; one good at fighting does not get angry; one good at defeating the enemy does not engage; one good at using people places himself below them. This is called the virtue of not contending, the power of using people, matching heaven: the highest principle of old.

t: Those who use troops have a saying
y: 用兵有言：吾不敢為主而為客，不敢進寸而退尺。是謂行無行，攘無臂，扔無敵，執無兵。禍莫大於輕敵，輕敵幾喪吾寶。故抗兵相加，哀者勝矣。
x: Those who use troops have a saying: I dare not play the host but play the guest; I dare not advance an inch but retreat a foot. This is called marching without ranks, rolling up sleeves without arms, dragging without an enemy, holding without weapons. No disaster is greater than taking the enemy lightly; taking the enemy lightly almost costs me my treasures. So when opposing armies meet, the side that grieves will win.

t: My words are very easy to understand and very easy to…
y: 吾言甚易知，甚易行。天下莫能知，莫能行。言有宗，事有君。夫唯無知，是以不我知。知我者希，則我者貴。是以聖人被褐懷玉。
x: My words are very easy to understand and very easy to practice, yet no one in the world can understand them or practice them. Words have an ancestor; affairs have a master. It is only because people do not understand this that they do not understand me. Those who understand me are few, and so I am all the more prized. Therefore the sage wears coarse cloth and carries jade in his bosom.

t: To know that one does not know is best
y: 知不知，上；不知知，病。夫唯病病，是以不病。聖人不病，以其病病，是以不病。
x: To know that one does not know is best; not to know but think one knows is a sickness. Only by treating the sickness as sickness can one be free of it. The sage is free of the sickness because he treats the sickness as sickness; so he is free of it.

t: When the people do not fear authority, a great terror will…
y: 民不畏威，則大威至。無狎其所居，無厭其所生。夫唯不厭，是以不厭。是以聖人自知不自見，自愛不自貴。故去彼取此。
x: When the people do not fear authority, a great terror will come. Do not crowd their dwellings; do not oppress their livelihood. Only if they are not oppressed will they not grow weary. Therefore the sage knows himself but does not show himself; loves himself but does not exalt himself. So he rejects that and takes this.

t: Courage in daring leads to death
y: 勇於敢則殺，勇於不敢則活。此兩者，或利或害。天之所惡，孰知其故？是以聖人猶難之。天之道，不爭而善勝，不言而善應，不召而自來，繟然而善謀。天網恢恢，疏而不失。
x: Courage in daring leads to death; courage in not daring leads to life. Of these two, one benefits and one harms. What heaven hates, who knows why? Therefore even the sage treats it as difficult. The Way of heaven does not contend yet is good at winning, does not speak yet is good at answering, is not summoned yet comes of itself, is unhurried yet good at planning. Heaven's net is vast; its mesh is wide, yet nothing slips through.

t: If the people do not fear death, how can you frighten them…
y: 民不畏死，奈何以死懼之？若使民常畏死，而為奇者，吾得執而殺之，孰敢？常有司殺者殺。夫代司殺者殺，是謂代大匠斲。夫代大匠斲者，希有不傷其手矣。
x: If the people do not fear death, how can you frighten them with death? If the people always feared death, and those who did strange things I could seize and kill, who would dare? There is always an executioner who kills. To kill in place of the executioner is like cutting wood in place of the master carpenter. Of those who cut in place of the master carpenter, few avoid hurting their hands.

t: The people starve because those above them eat too much in…
y: 民之饑，以其上食稅之多，是以饑。民之難治，以其上之有為，是以難治。民之輕死，以其求生之厚，是以輕死。夫唯無以生為者，是賢於貴生。
x: The people starve because those above them eat too much in taxes; that is why they starve. The people are hard to govern because those above them meddle; that is why they are hard to govern. The people take death lightly because they seek life too eagerly; that is why they take death lightly. Only those who do not strive for life are wiser than those who prize life.

t: When people are alive they are soft and weak
y: 人之生也柔弱，其死也堅强。萬物草木之生也柔脆，其死也枯槁。故堅强者死之徒，柔弱者生之徒。是以兵强則不勝，木强則兵。强大處下，柔弱處上。
x: When people are alive they are soft and weak; when they die they are hard and stiff. Plants and trees, when alive, are soft and tender; when they die, they are dry and withered. So the hard and stiff are followers of death; the soft and weak are followers of life. Therefore an army that is too strong will not win; a tree that is too strong will be cut down. The strong and great take the lower place; the soft and weak take the higher.

t: The Way of heaven, is it not like stretching a bow?
y: 天之道，其猶張弓與？高者抑之，下者舉之；有餘者損之，不足者補之。天之道，損有餘而補不足。人之道則不然，損不足以奉有餘。孰能有餘以奉天下？唯有道者。是以聖人為而不恃，功成而不處，其不欲見賢。
x: The Way of heaven, is it not like stretching a bow? The high end is pressed down, the low end is raised; what is in excess is reduced, what is lacking is supplied. The Way of heaven reduces excess and supplies what is lacking. The way of man is not so: it reduces the lacking to serve those who have excess. Who can take his excess to serve the world? Only one who has the Way. Therefore the sage acts but does not rely on it, completes the work but does not dwell in it; he does not wish to show his worth.

t: Nothing in the world is softer and weaker than water, yet…
y: 天下莫柔弱於水，而攻堅强者莫之能勝，其無以易之。弱之勝强，柔之勝剛，天下莫不知，莫能行。是以聖人云：受國之垢，是謂社稷主；受國不祥，是為天下王。正言若反。
x: Nothing in the world is softer and weaker than water, yet for attacking the hard and strong nothing can surpass it, for nothing can take its place. That the weak overcomes the strong and the soft overcomes the hard, everyone in the world knows, yet no one can practice it. So the sage says: one who takes on the filth of the state is called the master of its altars; one who takes on the misfortunes of the state is the king of the world. True words seem contrary.

t: When a great resentment is reconciled, some resentment…
y: 和大怨，必有餘怨，安可以為善？是以聖人執左契，而不責於人。有德司契，無德司徹。天道無親，常與善人。
x: When a great resentment is reconciled, some resentment surely remains; how can that be counted good? Therefore the sage holds the left half of the tally and does not press others for payment. One who has virtue keeps to the tally; one without virtue keeps to collecting. The Way of heaven has no favorites; it is always with the good.

t: A small state with few people
y: 小國寡民。使有什伯之器而不用，使民重死而不遠徙。雖有舟輿，無所乘之；雖有甲兵，無所陳之。使人復結繩而用之。甘其食，美其服，安其居，樂其俗。鄰國相望，雞犬之聲相聞，民至老死不相往來。
x: A small state with few people. Let there be tools for tens and hundreds of men, yet not used; let the people take death seriously and not move far away. Though they have boats and carriages, they have no occasion to ride them; though they have armor and weapons, they have no occasion to display them. Let people return to knotting cords and using them. Let them find their food sweet, their clothes fine, their homes peaceful, their customs a joy. Neighboring states may be in sight of one another, and the sounds of their roosters and dogs may be heard, yet the people grow old and die without ever going back and forth.

t: Trustworthy words are not beautiful
y: 信言不美，美言不信。善者不辯，辯者不善。知者不博，博者不知。聖人不積，既以為人己愈有，既以與人己愈多。天之道，利而不害；聖人之道，為而不爭。
x: Trustworthy words are not beautiful; beautiful words are not trustworthy. The good do not argue; those who argue are not good. Those who know are not broad in learning; those broad in learning do not know. The sage does not hoard. The more he does for others, the more he has; the more he gives to others, the more he possesses. The Way of heaven benefits and does not harm; the Way of the sage acts and does not contend.

t: The right way to teach
y: 人之初，性本善，性相近，習相遠。苟不教，性乃遷，教之道，貴以專。昔孟母，擇鄰處，子不學，斷機杼。竇燕山，有義方，教五子，名俱揚。
x: At birth, people are good by nature. By nature they are close to one another; by practice they grow far apart. If they are not taught, that nature will change. In the way of teaching, what matters is steady focus. Long ago, Mencius's mother chose her neighbours with care. When her son would not study, she cut the cloth on her loom. Dou Yanshan had the right way of teaching. He taught his five sons, and every one of them made a name.

t: The father's fault
y: 養不教，父之過，教不嚴，師之惰。子不學，非所宜，幼不學，老何爲。
x: To raise a child without teaching is the father's fault. To teach without strictness is the teacher's neglect. For a child not to study is not as it should be. If one does not learn when young, what will one do when old?

t: Uncarved jade
y: 玉不琢，不成器，人不學，不知義。爲人子，方少時，親師友，習禮儀。
x: Jade that is not carved does not become a vessel. People who do not learn do not know what is right. As a son or daughter, while still young, keep close to teachers and friends and practise good manners.

t: A warmed bed and a pear given up
y: 香九齡，能溫席，孝於親，所當執。融四歲，能讓梨，弟於長，宜先知。首孝悌，次見聞，知某數，識某文。
x: Huang Xiang, at nine, warmed his father's bed. Devotion to parents is what everyone should hold to. Kong Rong, at four, gave up the bigger pear. Respect for elders should be learned early. First, devotion to parents and respect for elder brothers; then, wider knowledge. Learn to count; learn to read.

t: One to ten
y: 一而十，十而百，百而千，千而萬。三才者，天地人，三光者，日月星。三綱者，君臣義，父子親，夫婦順。
x: One to ten, ten to a hundred, a hundred to a thousand, a thousand to ten thousand. The Three Powers are Heaven, Earth and Humankind. The Three Lights are the sun, the moon and the stars. The Three Bonds: between ruler and minister, rightness; between father and son, closeness; between husband and wife, harmony.

t: Four seasons, four directions
y: 曰春夏，曰秋冬，此四時，運不窮。曰南北，曰西東，此四方，應乎中。
x: Spring and summer, autumn and winter: these four seasons turn without end. South and north, west and east: these four directions are reckoned from the centre.

t: Five Phases, Five Constants
y: 曰水火，木金土，此五行，本乎數。曰仁義，禮智信，此五常，不容紊。
x: Water and fire, wood, metal and earth: these Five Phases are rooted in number. Benevolence and rightness, propriety, wisdom and good faith: these Five Constants must not be thrown into disorder.

t: Six grains, six animals
y: 稻粱菽，麥黍稷，此六穀，人所食。馬牛羊，雞犬豕，此六畜，人所飼。
x: Rice and sorghum, beans, wheat, broomcorn millet and foxtail millet: these six grains are what people eat. Horse, ox and sheep, chicken, dog and pig: these six animals are what people raise.

t: Seven feelings, five colours
y: 曰喜怒，曰哀懼，愛惡欲，七情具。青赤黃，及黑白，此五色，目所識。酸苦甘，及辛鹹，此五味，口所含。羶焦香，及腥朽，此五臭，鼻所嗅。
x: Joy and anger, sorrow and fear, love, hate and desire: these seven feelings everyone has. Green, red and yellow, black and white: these five colours are what the eye can tell apart. Sour, bitter and sweet, pungent and salty: these five tastes are what the mouth can sense. Rank, scorched and fragrant, fishy and rotten: these five smells are what the nose can catch.

t: Eight sounds, four tones
y: 匏土革，木石金，絲與竹，乃八音。曰平上，曰去入，此四聲，宜調協。
x: Gourd, clay and hide, wood, stone and metal, silk and bamboo: these are the eight sounds. The level and the rising, the departing and the entering: these four tones should be kept in harmony.

t: Nine generations, ten duties
y: 高曾祖，父而身，身而子，子而孫。自子孫，至玄曾，乃九族，人之倫。父子恩，夫婦從，兄則友，弟則恭。長幼序，友與朋，君則敬，臣則忠。此十義，人所同。
x: Great-great-grandfather, great-grandfather, grandfather, father and oneself; then oneself to son, son to grandson. From son and grandson on to great-grandson and great-great-grandson: these are the nine generations, the order of human kinship. Between father and son, kindness; between husband and wife, accord. The elder brother is warm, the younger brother respectful. Between old and young, due order; between friends, friendship. The ruler is respectful, the minister loyal. These ten duties are shared by all people.

t: Teaching beginners
y: 凡訓蒙，須講究，詳訓故，明句讀。爲學者，必有初，小學終，至四書。
x: Whoever teaches beginners must take care: explain the words in detail, and make clear where the sentences break. Those who study must start at the beginning: finish the Elementary Learning, then go on to the Four Books.

t: The Four Books
y: 論語者，二十篇，羣弟子，記善言。孟子者，七篇止，講道德，說仁義。作中庸，子思筆，中不偏，庸不易。作大學，乃曾子，自修齊，至平治。
x: The Analects has twenty books, in which the disciples recorded the Master's good words. The Mencius ends at seven books. It speaks of the Way and virtue, of benevolence and rightness. The Doctrine of the Mean came from the brush of Zisi. “Mean” is not leaning; “constant” is not changing. The Great Learning was written by Zengzi. It runs from cultivating oneself and ordering one's family to governing the state and bringing peace to the world.

t: The Six Classics
y: 孝經通，四書熟，如六經，始可讀。詩書易，禮春秋，號六經，當講求。有連山，有歸藏，有周易，三易詳。
x: Once the Classic of Filial Piety is understood and the Four Books are well known, one can begin to read the Six Classics. The Odes, the Documents and the Changes, the Rites and the Spring and Autumn are called the Six Classics; they deserve close study. There was the Lianshan, there was the Guicang, there was the Zhou Changes: these are the Three Changes, set out in full.

t: The Documents and the Rites
y: 有典謨，有訓誥，有誓命，書之奧。我周公，作周禮，著六官，存治體。大小戴，注禮記，述聖言，禮樂備。
x: There are canons and counsels, instructions and announcements, oaths and commands: these are the depths of the Documents. Our Duke of Zhou wrote the Rites of Zhou, setting out the six ministries and preserving the framework of government. The Elder and Younger Dai annotated the Record of Rites, passing on the sages' words, and ritual and music were made complete.

t: The Odes and the Spring and Autumn
y: 曰國風，曰雅頌，號四詩，當諷詠。詩既亡，春秋作，寓褒貶，別善惡。三傳者，有公羊，有左氏，有穀梁。
x: The Airs of the States, the Greater and Lesser Elegantiae and the Hymns are called the four parts of the Odes; they should be chanted aloud. When the Odes had lost their force, the Spring and Autumn was written, with praise and blame tucked into its wording to tell good from bad. The three commentaries are the Gongyang, the Zuo and the Guliang.

t: The philosophers
y: 經既明，方讀子，撮其要，記其事。五子者，有荀揚，文中子，及老莊。
x: Once the Classics are clear, go on to the philosophers: pick out their main points and remember their stories. The five philosophers are Xunzi and Yang Xiong, Wenzhongzi, and Laozi and Zhuangzi.

t: Three Sovereigns, Two Emperors
y: 經子通，讀諸史，考世系，知終始。自羲農，至黃帝，號三皇，居上世。唐有虞，號二帝，相揖遜，稱盛世。
x: With Classics and philosophers mastered, read the histories: trace the lines of succession, and learn how each age began and ended. From Fuxi and Shennong to the Yellow Emperor: these are called the Three Sovereigns, and they belong to the remotest past. Yao of Tang and Shun of Yu are called the Two Emperors. They yielded the throne to one another with courtesy, and their age is called a golden one.

t: Xia, Shang and Zhou
y: 夏有禹，商有湯，周文武，稱三王。夏傳子，家天下，四百載，遷夏社。湯伐夏，國號商，六百載，至紂亡。周武王，始誅紂，八百載，最長久。
x: Xia had Yu, Shang had Tang, Zhou had Wen and Wu: these are called the Three Kings. Xia passed the throne to a son, and the realm became one family's possession. After four hundred years, the altar of Xia was moved. Tang overthrew Xia and named his state Shang. After six hundred years it fell under the tyrant Zhou. King Wu of Zhou began by putting the tyrant to death. His dynasty lasted eight hundred years, the longest of all.

t: From the Spring and Autumn to Qin
y: 周轍東，王綱墜，逞干戈，尚遊說。始春秋，終戰國，五霸強，七雄出。嬴秦氏，始兼併，傳二世，楚漢爭。
x: When Zhou moved its capital east, the king's authority collapsed. Men trusted in shield and spear and prized the travelling persuaders. It began with the Spring and Autumn and ended with the Warring States: the Five Hegemons grew strong, and the Seven Powers arose. The Ying house of Qin was the first to swallow up all the states. It passed to a second emperor, and then Chu and Han fought for the realm.

t: The two Han
y: 高祖興，漢業建，至孝平，王莽篡。光武興，爲東漢，四百年，終於獻。
x: Gaozu rose and founded the house of Han. Under Emperor Ping, Wang Mang seized the throne. Guangwu rose again and founded the Eastern Han. After four hundred years, Han ended with Emperor Xian.

t: Three Kingdoms to the Northern and Southern Dynasties
y: 魏蜀吳，爭漢鼎，號三國，迄兩晉。宋齊繼，梁陳承，爲南朝，都金陵。北元魏，分東西，宇文周，與高齊。
x: Wei, Shu and Wu fought over the Han throne. They are called the Three Kingdoms, and they lasted until the two Jin. Song and Qi followed, Liang and Chen came after: these were the Southern Dynasties, with their capital at Jinling. In the north, the Wei of the Yuan house split into East and West; then came the Zhou of the Yuwen and the Qi of the Gao.

t: Sui and Tang
y: 迨至隋，一土宇，不再傳，失統緒。唐高祖，起義師，除隋亂，創國基。二十傳，三百載，梁滅之，國乃改。
x: Then came Sui, which made the land one. It did not last past its second ruler and lost the line of succession. Gaozu of Tang raised a righteous army, cleared away the disorder of Sui and laid the foundations of his state. Twenty reigns over three hundred years; then Liang destroyed it, and the dynasty changed.

t: From the Five Dynasties to Song
y: 梁唐晉，及漢周，稱五代，皆有由。炎宋興，受周禪，十八傳，南北混。
x: Liang, Tang and Jin, and then Han and Zhou: these are called the Five Dynasties, and each had a reason for its name. The fiery Song arose, receiving the throne from Zhou. Over eighteen reigns, north and south fell into turmoil.

t: Liao, Jin and Yuan
y: 遼與金，皆稱帝，元滅金，絕宋世。輿圖廣，超前代，九十年，國祚廢。
x: Liao and Jin both called their rulers emperors. Yuan destroyed Jin and put an end to the Song. Its territory was vast, beyond any earlier dynasty, yet after ninety years its mandate was gone.

t: Ming
y: 太祖興，國大明，號洪武，都金陵。迨成祖，遷燕京，十六世，至崇禎。權閹肆，寇如林，李闖出，神器焚。
x: Taizu arose and named his state the Great Ming. His reign was called Hongwu, and his capital was Jinling. Then the Yongle Emperor moved the capital to Yanjing. Sixteen reigns later came Chongzhen. Powerful eunuchs ran riot, rebels were as thick as a forest; Li the Dashing King rose up, and the throne went up in flames.

t: Qing and the Republic
y: 清順治，據神京，至十傳，宣統遜。舉總統，共和成，復漢土，民國興。
x: Shunzhi of the Qing took the capital. Ten reigns later, Xuantong gave up the throne. A president was elected and the republic was made; Han rule was restored over the land, and the Republic of China arose.

t: What history is for
y: 廿二史，全在茲，載治亂，知興衰。讀史者，考實錄，通古今，若親目。口而誦，心而惟，朝於斯，夕於斯。
x: The Twenty-two Histories all are here, recording order and disorder so that we know why states rise and fall. Whoever reads history should study the true records, linking past and present as if seeing it with their own eyes. Recite it with your mouth and think it through in your mind, in the morning and again at night.

t: Even Confucius learned
y: 昔仲尼，師項橐，古聖賢，尚勤學。趙中令，讀魯論，彼既仕，學且勤。
x: Long ago Confucius took Xiang Tuo as a teacher. The sages of old still studied hard. Zhao, the chief secretary, read the Analects. Though already in high office, he kept studying diligently.

t: Learning without books
y: 披蒲編，削竹簡，彼無書，且知勉。頭懸樑，錐刺股，彼不教，自勤苦。
x: One copied texts onto woven rushes, another shaved bamboo strips to write on. They had no books, yet still pushed themselves to learn. One tied his hair to a roof beam, another jabbed his thigh with an awl. No one made them study; they drove themselves.

t: Learning in poverty
y: 如囊螢，如映雪，家雖貧，學不輟。如負薪，如掛角，身雖勞，猶苦卓。
x: One read by a bag of fireflies, another by the light off the snow. Though their families were poor, they never stopped learning. One read while carrying firewood, another hung his book on an ox's horn. Though their bodies were worn out, they still worked hard and stood firm.

t: Learning late in life
y: 蘇老泉，二十七，始發憤，讀書籍。彼既老，猶悔遲，爾小生，宜早思。若梁灝，八十二，對大廷，魁多士。彼既成，衆稱異，爾小生，宜立志。
x: Su Laoquan was twenty-seven when he first resolved to study and set himself to his books. Even when he was old, he regretted starting late. You who are young should think of this early. Liang Hao was eighty-two when he answered at the palace examination and came first among all the scholars. When he succeeded, everyone marvelled. You who are young should set your aim now.

t: Learning while young
y: 瑩八歲，能詠詩，泌七歲，能賦棋。彼穎悟，人稱奇，爾幼學，當效之。
x: Ying was eight when he could recite poems; Mi was seven when he could write on the game of go. They were quick and bright, and people called them remarkable. You who are studying young should follow their example.

t: Girls learn too
y: 蔡文姬，能辨琴，謝道韞，能詠吟。彼女子，且聰敏，爾男子，當自警。
x: Cai Wenji could tell the notes of the zither; Xie Daoyun could chant and compose verse. They were girls, and yet so clever. You boys should take this as a spur to yourselves.

t: Whoever strives can do the same
y: 唐劉晏，方七歲，舉神童，作正字。彼雖幼，身已仕，爾幼學，勉而致。有爲者，亦若是。
x: Liu Yan of Tang, at just seven, was chosen as a child prodigy and made a text corrector. Though he was young, he already held office. You who are studying young can get there too with effort. Whoever strives can do the same.

t: The dog keeps watch, the silkworm spins
y: 犬守夜，雞司晨，苟不學，曷爲人。蠶吐絲，蜂釀蜜，人不學，不如物。
x: The dog keeps watch at night, the rooster announces the dawn. If you do not learn, how can you call yourself human? The silkworm spins silk, the bee makes honey. People who do not learn fall short even of these creatures.

t: Learn when young, act when grown
y: 幼而學，壯而行，上致君，下澤民。揚名聲，顯父母，光於前，裕於後。人遺子，金滿籝，我教子，惟一經。
x: Learn when young, act when grown: above, serve your ruler; below, do good to the people. Make your name known and bring honour to your parents; add glory to those before you and leave plenty to those after. Others leave their children a chest full of gold. I teach my children only one classic.

t: Take heed
y: 勤有功，戲無益，戒之哉，宜勉力。
x: Diligence brings results; play brings no profit. Take heed, and put your strength into it.
